name: Brian Harris

arrival.reason: with their family as a child

backstory: A mother on nights mopping hospital corridors, and a suitcase he was told was for the coast, not for leaving. Since the move he has not felt at home anywhere, so he has made himself everyone's neighbour instead: waving at every window, knowing whose bins go out on which day, saying yes before he has checked the diary. The sweeping is the only care he gives his own front step. What he keeps from the people around him is money: rented flats bought under his own name with redundancy money, and savings far beyond what the street assumes. He calls himself ordinary because it keeps people comfortable, and he does not like being leaned on. He wants everyone to like him. What he needs is for one person to see him properly, and that is the person he has held furthest away.
persona: He has the chairs out for quiz night a week early and knows whose bins go out on which day without being asked. He turns down a friend's painting class with a laugh and no reason, and goes short with anyone who offers to carry his shopping. A box of keys from the old house is still unopened in the hall, under the coats.
speaking_style: He talks fast and cheerfully, in plain, polite, old-fashioned phrases. 'Right then' is his stop-gap whenever a question turns personal. He states things as settled fact and almost never says 'I think'. He taps the table lightly when he is making a point.
mannerisms: explains things at length before reaching the point
reminds listeners that the old way has never let anyone down

past.content: Mum told me the suitcase was for the coast, and I believed her until I saw Dad's shaving kit go in after it.

The chair in the day unit had a dent worn into its left arm, and I pressed my thumb into it for six hours at a time. I've been clear for years now, but I still look for that dent when I walk past a hospital.
Every Thursday I meant to start the walk again, and the blood pressure book sat in the drawer under the phone with no new numbers in it.

hooks.description: He has a letter from the friend he knew before the move that he never answered, and he has been too ashamed to say he lost his nerve.
He once got a rival at work written up over a missed call log, and he still tells the story as if he was the one who spotted the error first.

voice.description: An American accent. A man in his late fifties. Medium-low pitch, warm and slightly gravelly timbre, unhurried but bright pace, friendly and plain-spoken in manner.
voice.reference_line: I spent most of my working life answering calls from people who had lost a card, a parcel, or their patience.
